zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0, https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . The transcription and explanatory notes here are scan-based editorial work, not a copy of that index.

lines.note: Wazawaza here denotes the several works or occupations associated with different people or social states. The final varias modifies the nouns continued below; its round final s replaces OCR variar.
Completes the occupations gloss with people and estates or conditions. The printed peßoas and eſtados are retained with their historical types.
Wazawazato is equated with wazato, deliberately or on purpose. The scan has the repeated uaza sequence, not the OCR form Vazatazato.
Completes de industria, meaning intentionally or by design, as the second Portuguese paraphrase of wazawazato.
Wazuka and wazukana describe something small in amount; Latin l introduces the adjectival alternative. The evaluation continues on the next row.
Completes the description of wazuka as of little consequence or importance, alongside small quantity.
Wazukani is explicitly an adverb: little or scarcely. The Portuguese abbreviation Adu. belongs to the italic apparatus.
Wazukani hyaku ni tarazu means falling only a little short of one hundred. The damaged penultimate consonant of tarazu supports z, while OCR tarauu gives neither the form nor the negative sense.
Completes faltaua pouco pera cento, a small shortfall from a hundred, confirming the negative tarazu above.

The verb wazurau means falling ill or being ill; the printed principal forms retain the contracted long vowel in ǒ and ǒta. The abraded headword is read Vazzurai from its surviving strokes and the repeated stem below; OCR Vatzurai misread the damaged z.
Me and zutsuu introduce eye illness and headache as examples of wazurau. The scan includes the opening paragraph sign omitted by OCR; the long-vowel notation in zzutçǔ is retained.

runs.text: doente dos olhos, ou de enxaqueca, &c. Item,

lines.note: Completes estar with eye disease or migraine. The damaged middle of enxaqueca can still be identified from its surviving q and surrounding strokes; the OCR space and p are misleading.

runs.text: junto com outros verbos de cuidar, &c ſig-

lines.note: The entry now explains compounds with verbs of thinking or worrying. Sig- begins significa on the next physical row; the printed abbreviation and line break are retained.

Completes significa and explains the compound sense as affliction or perplexity. Perplexidade has an abraded medial p, rather than OCR perlexidade. The Japanese example begins An- and continues below.

An- plus jivazzu ǒ introduces anxious deliberation, followed by omoi wazurau. The expected r before the first ǒ is not securely visible in the damaged gap, so the provisional spaced reading remains rather than supplying it. Xiua- begins shiwazurau across the row boundary.

runs.text: Eſtar com amão na obra duuidoſo,

lines.note: Completes shiwazurau, explained as having one’s hand in the work while remaining doubtful. The joined amão is retained as printed, with the discussion of hesitation continued below.

runs.text: & perpleco do que farà, ou como farà

lines.note: The hesitation concerns what one will do or how to do it. The printed perpleco and grave accents in farà are preserved without modernizing the Portuguese spelling.
The noun wazurai means illness, and also expense or trouble. The first V is slanted in this impression; the existing isolated italic marking is retained.

Wazuraigachina and wazuraigachini gozaru describe susceptibility to frequent illness. The second compound is continuous in the scan, correcting the OCR gap before achini; gozaru is divided at the row end.
Zaru completes gozaru. The Portuguese confirms frequent or habitual sickness, and the weak middle of doente is not a lexical space.
Wazurai-gao describes the face or appearance of a sick person. The gloss reads Roſto, with t rather than OCR i; no modernization of the existing long-s convention is imposed.
Wazurawashii is glossed here through being ill or indisposed. The printed abbreviation doẽte is retained, and the following rows supply related nominal and adverbial forms.
Wazurawashisa is the corresponding abstract noun, the condition described by the preceding adjective. This short form is its own physical row.

This is the adverbial form corresponding to wazurawashii. The expected u after Vazz is heavily abraded and not securely recovered, so the supplied gap is retained as a nonblocking diplomatic uncertainty.
Wazurooshii is referred back to the preceding adjective by Idem. The visible caron on ǒ is retained rather than regularizing the vowel to the other form.

Uba is here the kinship term grandmother, separately from the following old-woman entry. The printed Auǒ has a caron-like two-stroke mark, retained without replacing it with the conventional modern Portuguese accent.
The second uba is glossed simply as an old woman. The adjacent identical headwords distinguish lexical meanings without adding unprinted Japanese characters.
Ubaguchi means an old woman’s mouth; the next sense names a vessel by resemblance. Item is visible, correcting OCR Irem, and Hum begins its Portuguese description.

runs.text: caldeirão que tem a boca deſta feição de boca

lines.note: The vessel is a cauldron whose opening resembles the mouth described below. The scan supports caldeirão and the repeated boca, not OCR caIdeirão and baca.
Completes the comparison with a toothless old woman’s mouth. This is the explanation of the vessel shape, not an additional headword.
The verb ubau means taking by force. The carons in the contracted principal forms bǒ and ǒta are retained as visible; the second form includes the b of the stem.
Ubaitori means seizing or taking away, referred to the same forceful-taking gloss. The printed otta is the past-form ending of toru.

runs.text: Principio, ou nacimento. Mas não ſe

lines.note: Ubu denotes beginning or birth. The Portuguese qualification starts here and continues below; the final ſe has long s, not the OCR f.

runs.text: vſa porſi ſe não compoſto. Vt,

lines.note: The entry says ubu is not used by itself, only in compounds. Vbuguinu is the first example, and the usage statement is preserved with its historical spacing.
Ubuguinu denotes the cloths or swaddling clothes of a newborn. The paragraph sign then introduces ubu-yu, divided at the physical row boundary.

runs.text: Aquella primeira agoa quente com que

lines.note: Yu completes ubuyu: the first warm water used to wash a newborn. The Portuguese relative clause continues below.
Completes the newborn’s washing, then introduces ubuya, the house or room of childbirth. The article before criança is a, not OCR e.
Completes the description of ubuya as the place where the child is born. This brief continuation retains its own physical-line identity.

runs.text: Doença de ar que dà à criança em

lines.note: Ubukaze is explained as an illness attributed to air affecting a newborn. The dictionary’s description is historical; it is not a modern diagnosis. The lower-case opening is retained from the supplied reading.
Completes em nacendo, on being born; ubukaze wo hiku is then the example of contracting this illness. The object particle remains attached in the printed form.
Completes dar este ar à criança, the Portuguese description of the newborn being affected by the illness.

Ubukami is followed by the preferred form ubu no kami. The Latin marker has the function of potius, but the expected t is not securely visible across the diagonal paper flaw: poiùs retains the surviving sequence and the grave above u. Cami in the Portuguese gloss names the birth deity.

runs.text: nacimento dos gentios que he como ſeu Anjo

lines.note: The birth deity is described in the missionaries’ terminology as the gentiles’ equivalent of a guardian angel. The scan supports nacimento and gentios, correcting OCR narimento and gotios.
Da guarda completes Anjo da guarda, the Christian analogy used for the Japanese protective deity.

runs.text: Cabello com que as crianças nacem

lines.note: This second ubukami means the hair with which babies are born. Com is damaged by the diagonal paper flaw but fits the surviving strokes and the relative clause; the entry begins at the ordinary headword margin.
The newborn hair is defined before anyone cuts or shaves it. The ending -rem of troſquiarem is weakened by the diagonal flaw; the plural verb pairs with raparem.

Ubukasa, ubugasa, and ubuse name the crusts on a newborn’s head, continued in column 2. An expected second Latin l before vbuxe is not securely visible through the diagonal flaw; the supplied punctuation is retained rather than supplying that letter. Bustellas has no terminal hyphen.

runs.text: da cabeça com que nacem as crianças.

lines.note: Completes Bustellas from column 1: the crusts on the head with which children are born. Crianças is legible despite the OCR substitution criarças.

runs.text: Aprimeira voz com que chora o

lines.note: Ubukoe is the first cry of a newborn. The scan supports chora, cries, rather than OCR chara; Aprimeira retains the tight printed joining supplied in the baseline.
Completes the newborn’s first-cry definition. The printed historical minino is preserved rather than modernized to menino.
Ubugasa refers back to ubukasa, the newborn scalp crusts explained across the column boundary. Vide is the italic cross-reference instruction.
Ubugi and ubuki are the newborn’s swaddling clothes. A weak initial v is visible in the alternative vbuqi, missing in the OCR buqi; the Portuguese description continues below.
Completes the account of cloths wrapped around a child at birth. The surviving strokes support criança and continuous nacendo, correcting the OCR loss and spurious gap.
Ubuguinu and ubukinu have the same newborn-clothing sense. The alternative is vbuqinu, supported by its own cross-reference below, not the OCR noise vhnqiru.

runs.text: Alma perdida que fica de pois, como

lines.note: Ubume is introduced through the historical belief in a dead mother’s lingering soul. Alma and como are recovered from the scan rather than OCR Alna and tome; de pois remains visibly separated.

runs.text: cuidão os gentios, da molher que morreo de

lines.note: The definition explicitly attributes the belief to the people called gentios by the missionaries. It concerns a woman who died, with the cause completed on the next row.
The death occurred in childbirth. The regional form ugume is then given for Ximo; the location name occurs inside the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Cami do nacimento que os gentios

lines.note: Ubu no kami again names the birth deity. Cami is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese gloss, and a real word separation is retained between os and gentios.

runs.text: venerão como ſeu Anjo da guarda.

lines.note: Completes the explanation that the deity is venerated like a guardian angel, repeating the analogy made in column 1.

runs.text: Penugem, ou cabelos do corpo da cri-

lines.note: Ubuke denotes down or fine body hair on a child. The final cri- begins criança on the following row.

After completing criança, the entry gives the figurative phrase ubuke no nukenu hito, a person whose infant down has not yet fallen away. The scan supports q in nuqenu, not OCR o, and the final hito is divided between rows.

runs.text: Homem que ainda eſtà nouo, & igno-

lines.note: To completes hito. The Portuguese figurative interpretation is someone still new and inexperienced, with ignorante continued below.
Completes ignorante em alguma cousa, specifying inexperience in a particular matter. The visible nasal abbreviation in algũa is retained.
Ubukinu refers upward to ubuguinu, the newborn-clothing entry. Supra belongs to the Latin cross-reference apparatus.

runs.text: Cami que guarda o lugar onde hum

lines.note: Ubusuna names the deity guarding the place where a person was born. The headword has b rather than OCR p, and the compressed right-end word is hum.
Completes the birthplace description, then supplies ubushina as the Ximo form. Ximo is part of the Portuguese regional explanation.
Ubuse refers to ubukasa, the infant scalp-crust term. The short cross-reference is a complete entry on its physical row.
Ubushina refers to ubusuna, explicitly connecting the regional form to the birthplace deity entry.

runs.text: Caſa do nacimento, ou que ſe faz pe-

lines.note: Ubuya is the house of childbirth, or one made for a birth to take place. The damaged compressed ending begins pera, continued by ra below, rather than OCR fazio.
Ra completes pera: the place is prepared so that someone may be born there. The line belongs to the ubuya definition.

runs.text: Agoa quente com que lauão a criança

lines.note: Ubuyu is the warm water in which a newborn is washed. Criança is printed at the compressed right edge, replacing OCR crisça.
Completes the bathing-water definition with the timing, at birth. The short line remains an independent physical row.

runs.text: Vcabe, uru, eta. l, vcame, uru.

lines.note: Ukabe and ukame are alternative verb stems for causing something to float. The Portuguese nadar is divided after na-, not the OCR nu.

runs.text: dar, ou ter ſobre a agoa. ¶

lines.note: Completes nadar and adds holding something on the water. Fune wo ukaburu illustrates floating a boat; its verb begins vca-, correcting OCR vo-.

Buru completes ukaburu, translated as making the boat float. Fune is explicitly embedded in the Portuguese sentence. The next example begins hito wo; its first o is abraded but visible as a rounded remnant, correcting OCR Fituo.
The figurative application to a person means saving someone. The scan supports the final u of vcaburu and a marked long u in Chǔ-, which begins the memorization example below.
Chuu ni mono wo ukaburu, alternatively ukamuru, means knowing something by heart in the accompanying gloss. The final Portuguese word is Saber, not OCR Sabr.
Completes the memorization gloss as knowing something by heart. Ukabeta hito then describes a person with such knowledge; the H in the divided Homem is visible at the compressed edge.

runs.text: mem que ſabe bem algũa couſa como de còr.

lines.note: Completes Homem and explains a person who knows a matter thoroughly, as if by heart. The right-end còr is readable, not OCR ir.
Ukameta yoo ni mono wo yuu hito describes someone who speaks as though he had mastered the subject. The scan separates monouo from yǔ, correcting the OCR split within the latter.

runs.text: mem, que pratica as couſas como que as ſoubeſſe

lines.note: Completes Homem: he discusses matters as if he knew them. The scan has pratica and the full final ſoubeſſe within the row, rather than OCR prattca and an inferred division.

runs.text: muito bem, não as ſabendo na verdade bem.

lines.note: Completes the contrast: the man speaks with apparent mastery although he does not actually know the matters well. The long s in ſabendo replaces OCR f, and the closing mark is a period rather than a hyphen.

runs.text: Vcabi, u, ǒda. l, vcami, u.

lines.note: Ukabi and ukami give the corresponding intransitive floating forms. The gloss begins the state of an object, completed by its position on the water below.
Completes being afloat; the second sense is to be saved or escape. This pairs with the preceding transitive verb’s figurative saving sense.
Ukabiide means rising or coming out on top of the water. The printed ij sequence is preserved as the historical spelling of the compound.

The verb ukagau is asking or inquiring into a superior’s wishes; its printed ǒ and ǒta retain the contracted long vowel. The compressed final võ- is the nasal abbreviation beginning vontade, not OCR oo.
Completes vontade de pessoa mais alta. Shiro no yoojin then begins an example about the watch or precautions of a fortress; the marked yǒ-, not OCR jb-, is visible.
Completes shiro no yoojin no yoo wo ukagau, observing the manner of a fortress’s watch. The Portuguese has eſpreitar, with the compressed final r before a, rather than OCR eſpreita.

runs.text: maneira que ha de vigiar a fortaleza. ¶

lines.note: Completes the explanation about watching the fortress. The new Japanese example starts Fi-, the first part of fima, and is roman rather than part of the preceding Portuguese gloss.

Fi- plus ma gives hima; bin hima wo ukagau concerns seeking a suitable opportunity. The scan contains bin without the extra final i of OCR bini. Conjunção is the Portuguese circumstance or conjunction of conditions.
Completes the opportunity-and-time explanation. Sho wo, referring to writings or a book, begins the next example; the weak rounded letter after X is o, supplying Xouo rather than the OCR Xuo.

runs.text: Ler, ou reuoluer, & buſcar o que

lines.note: The book example is explained as reading, reviewing, and looking up what one has learned. The expected a in vcagǒ falls in a genuine abraded gap; vc gǒ is retained rather than silently supplying a lost letter.

runs.text: hum tem lido, ou aprendido em algum liuro.

lines.note: Completes the reference to what a person has read or learned in a book. The right-edge liuro contains r, omitted by OCR liuo.

Ukagaimi means searching or looking attentively, with consideração begun at the line end. No paragraph sign precedes this headword in the scan. The isolated ſideração below is treated as a catchword; the following page is not supplied to verify its repetition.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The final B in the second running header is badly abraded; its remaining stem and bowls support B. The bottom fragment is assigned to the catchword from its isolated far-right position below the last regular row; the following page is not included for comparison.
